title: Belonging: Friends, Loneliness and Bullying
reflection: When my child says “nobody”, can I meet the feeling first, before I answer it?

questions.q: Which test does Lesson 19 give for telling whether a parent’s holding on has crossed from care into binding?
o: Whether the child obeys the limits willingly, or only after some argument.
Does this belonging widen the child’s world, or does it narrow it?
Whether the child’s friends are of the same values as the family’s own.
Whether the parent feels anxious, or at ease, as the child grows older.
questions.e: A simple test serves for any limit, worry or “no”: does this belonging widen the child’s world, or narrow it? Hold close with an open hand: a warm, unconditional home as the base, and a door that opens outward as the child grows. Two helpful questions: whose need is this limit serving, the child’s growth or the parent’s own worry?
questions.c: Hold close with an open hand

questions.q: A ten-year-old tells her grandmother that nobody sat with her at lunch, and the grandmother says, “But you have lots of friends!” The girl says, “Never mind.” Which approach fits Lesson 19?
o: Explain that friendships change, and that she will soon find new ones.
Point out how many friends she has, and name them to prove the point.
Tell her that everyone belongs to the whole, so no one is ever really alone.
Meet the feeling first, “that sounds lonely”, then ask open questions side by side.
questions.e: “But you have lots of friends” tells the child she has not been heard. The disappointment comes first: “that sounds lonely.” Over toast, side by side, in the car or on a walk, a few open questions: what happened, what did it feel like, what would help. Then, when the child is ready, the wider view comes gently: this feeling is a wave, and it passes.
questions.c: Meet the feeling first, then widen the view

questions.q: Why does the lesson say that “we all belong to the whole” is never an answer to a child’s hurt at being left out?
o: The felt belonging comes first, and the widening grows from a secure centre.
Children cannot understand an idea so large until they are much older.
The idea is true only for those who already hold the Vedantic view.
It would lead the child to think the hurt is of no importance at all.
questions.e: The felt belonging comes first, and the widening follows. It grows from a secure centre and never takes its place. A child who has not yet been held by a few cannot yet embrace the many. The highest view is the goal of growing, not the starting point of the journey, which begins with a family that is real and precious.
questions.c: Felt belonging first; the widening grows from it

questions.q: A mother’s seventeen-year-old daughter lost her best friend last term with no quarrel, says she is “fine” and stays in her room. Which approach fits Lesson 19?
o: Insist that she join a club, so that new friends will soon take the place of the old.
Leave her alone, since a seventeen-year-old needs to work these things out.
Sit near, say little, and offer one door; see a doctor or counsellor if she stays low.
Talk to the friend’s parents, so that the two girls can be brought together again.
questions.e: Widening the circle works by invitation: a push says “something is wrong with you”, while an invitation says “here is a door, and you may choose.” Friendships tend to grow around something shared, and side by side is easier than face to face. If it lasts, or a young person seems low or withdrawn, the family doctor or a counsellor is the right door.
questions.c: Invite, never push; seek help if it lasts

questions.q: “A quiet child who prefers time alone is probably lonely, and should be encouraged firmly into groups.”
questions.e: Being alone is a fact; feeling lonely is an ache. A person can be alone and at peace, and can feel lonely in a crowd. The quiet child has real gifts: depth, careful watching, steadiness and a few loyal friendships. What matters is how the child comes back from time alone and with others, lighter or heavier, and the child’s own account is the best guide.
questions.c: Alone is a fact; lonely is an ache

questions.q: A child tells her mother that several children have been hurting her on purpose, week after week. Which response fits Lesson 19?
o: Teach her to rise above it, and to grow stronger by looking within herself.
Wait a fortnight to see if it stops, and then go to speak to the school.
Welcome the telling, say it is not her fault, and tell the school at once.
Speak to the parents of the other children, and ask them all to put a stop to it.
questions.e: Safety first, and then a home where telling is safe: a soft face, “I’m really glad you told me”, listening fully, and the plain words “you are not in trouble, and this is not your fault.” The school is told without waiting; keep a short note of what happened, when and who saw it, and keep asking what the school will do. Strengthening goes together with protecting.
questions.c: Safety first, tell the school at once

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the “feedback” idea, that a hurt can show us where to grow, is never a verdict?
o: Because a child cannot be held responsible for what other children do to her.
Because the child is hurt first, and hears plainly that it is not her fault.
Because inner growth can happen only when the outer problem is gone.
Because looking inward is a matter for the adult, not for the child.
questions.e: A hurt child hears the hurt first, and hears plainly that it is not their fault and that the one who harms is responsible. Only then is the strengthening offered, as a power: “you can grow stronger through this.” Looking inward is never instead of asking the school to stop the harm; strengthening goes together with protecting.
questions.c: Feedback is never a verdict; protect as well as strengthen

questions.q: A parent learns that her daughter has been among those leaving a girl out and laughing at her. Which response fits Lesson 19?
o: Stay with her in love, insist the harm stops and is repaired, and hear the school out.
Find out the reason behind it, and treat that reason before anything else is done.
Tell her that this is not who she really is, and say no more about it afterwards.
Ask the school to handle it, since the parent’s part is only to support the school’s work.
questions.e: The hurt is real and needs to stop, and the child is more than what she has done, as the sky is more than the weather. The behaviour stops, the harm is repaired, and the child learns another way. The parent need not know the reason to act, and listens to the school without defending. Holy Mother’s stance, “What wrong can children do?”, is love that does not withdraw.
questions.c: Love does not withdraw; the harm stops and is repaired

questions.q: “A child who bullies must feel small inside, so low self-esteem is the usual cause.”
questions.e: Dr Watson: the research is more mixed than that. Some children who bully do struggle, but across studies there is little support for low self-esteem as the usual cause. Some seem quite socially skilled, and some are well placed in their group. A parent cannot assume a reason, nor does a parent need the reason in order to act.
questions.c: A parent need not know the reason in order to act

questions.q: A seventeen-year-old says of a bullying incident she watched, “I just stood there,” and feels ashamed. Which response fits Lesson 19?
o: Tell her it was not her business, and that she did right to keep well clear of it.
Say that standing by was as bad as joining in, and so she must put it right at once.
Help her find small acts within reach, and talk through what the family would do.
Ask her to confront those who did it, so that she learns courage that way.
questions.e: Silence feels safe, and it is not entirely so. Small acts are within reach: not joining in, sitting beside the one left out, a kind word afterwards, telling a trusted adult, which is kindness and not tale-telling. A family can talk it through at the table beforehand: what would we do? The courage grows in small steps.
questions.c: The watcher grows in courage through small acts
